questions.question: Steven Koonin served as Undersecretary for Science at the US Department of Energy under President Obama, leading the department's climate-science assessment work. In 2021 he published *Unsettled: What Climate Science Tells Us, What It Doesn't, and Why It Matters*. He argued the IPCC's own technical reports do not actually support the catastrophist framing that news coverage routinely puts on top of them. What is Koonin's central claim?
questions.answer: Earth is warming and humans contribute — but the headline-catastrophe framing is layered on top of the technical reports, not drawn from them
choices: Earth is warming and humans contribute — but the headline-catastrophe framing is layered on top of the technical reports, not drawn from them
Earth is not warming at all — and the entire field of climate science is a politically constructed hoax with no honest researchers in it
Earth is warming faster than any IPCC report admits — and the actual catastrophe will arrive sooner than even the alarmist coverage suggests
Earth is warming as predicted — and there is no remaining gap between what the IPCC reports say and what the press accurately conveys to readers
questions.context: Koonin's book draws on the IPCC AR5 and US National Climate Assessment to show that hurricanes have not increased, US heatwaves are no worse than the 1930s Dust Bowl, sea-level rise has not accelerated meaningfully versus the early 20th century, and Greenland's ice mass is roughly where it was in the 1940s. He argues the gap between technical reports and media framing is the actual scandal — not warming itself, which he accepts.

questions.question: When Steven Koonin's *Unsettled* (2021) appeared, much of the response from establishment climate commentary tried to discredit him personally rather than engage his specific evidentiary claims. Critics called him a 'denier' and dismissed him as unqualified. What were Koonin's actual credentials?
questions.answer: Caltech theoretical-physics professor and provost, BP's chief scientist, then Undersecretary for Science at DOE under Obama — credentials more elite than nearly all of his critics
choices: Caltech theoretical-physics professor and provost, BP's chief scientist, then Undersecretary for Science at DOE under Obama — credentials more elite than nearly all of his critics
Caltech undergraduate degree only, no graduate work and no published research record — credentials the press correctly described as inadequate for the subject
Caltech administrator with no scientific training of any kind, working purely in management and fundraising — credentials properly questioned by reviewers
Caltech faculty in literature and rhetoric, with no physics background or any government science experience — credentials the press accurately characterized
questions.context: Koonin earned his PhD in theoretical physics at MIT in 1975, joined Caltech's faculty, became provost (the chief academic officer), served as BP's chief scientist 2004-2009, then DOE Undersecretary for Science under Obama 2009-2011. His scientific bona fides put him near the top of the field. The pattern — dismissing dissenters as 'unqualified' regardless of their actual credentials — is one of the bank's recurring themes about how dissent gets suppressed.

questions.question: *Unsettled* (2021) draws its strongest evidence not from skeptic blogs but from the IPCC's own technical chapters and the US National Climate Assessment — the official reports themselves. Koonin lists several specific claims media coverage routinely repeats that the underlying reports do NOT actually support. Which set best captures Koonin's documented examples?
questions.answer: Hurricanes haven't increased, US heatwaves aren't worse than the 1930s, sea-level rise hasn't meaningfully accelerated, Greenland ice mass is near 1940s levels — all from the official reports
choices: Hurricanes haven't increased, US heatwaves aren't worse than the 1930s, sea-level rise hasn't meaningfully accelerated, Greenland ice mass is near 1940s levels — all from the official reports
Hurricanes have doubled, US heatwaves are unprecedented, sea levels rose 10 feet in the last decade, Greenland has lost half its ice — all confirmed in the reports
Hurricanes are extinct, US heatwaves never happen, sea levels are dropping yearly, Greenland is gaining ice rapidly — all clearly stated in the official documents
Hurricanes are unmeasurable, US heatwaves are unrecorded, sea levels are unknown, Greenland ice is unstudied — none of which the reports actually address
questions.context: Koonin cites IPCC AR5 WG1 directly: 'low confidence' that hurricane intensity has increased; US heatwaves of the 1930s Dust Bowl exceed modern records by most measures; satellite altimetry shows sea-level rise rates similar to the early 20th century within measurement uncertainty; Greenland's ice mass trends have moved up and down across decades. The contrast between these technical findings and routine media catastrophism is the book's organizing argument.

questions.question: John Cook's 2013 paper in *Environmental Research Letters* is the most-cited source for the '97% of scientists agree' claim. Cook's team reviewed about 12,000 climate-paper abstracts. The headline figure is famous — but the methodological move that produced it is the contested step. What did the 97% number actually MEASURE?
questions.answer: 97% of the ~32% of abstracts that took any position on cause endorsed human contribution — saying nothing about how much, whether catastrophic, or what policy follows
choices: 97% of the ~32% of abstracts that took any position on cause endorsed human contribution — saying nothing about how much, whether catastrophic, or what policy follows
97% of every climate scientist in the world personally endorsed every IPCC catastrophe scenario — and every proposed policy response by name
97% of all 12,000 abstracts explicitly named humans as the primary cause — and predicted imminent catastrophe within a definite timeframe
97% of randomly polled non-scientist members of the public said they believed climate scientists — about every aspect of the topic
questions.context: Cook's team classified about 12,000 abstracts. About two-thirds took no position on cause at all. Of the third that did, 97% endorsed at least some human contribution — a claim almost no one disputes, including Koonin and most other named skeptics. The slide from 'humans contribute' to 'humans are the primary cause' to 'imminent catastrophe' to 'specific policy X must be adopted' happens in the press, not in the underlying data.

questions.question: The famous '97% of scientists agree' headline derives from John Cook's 2013 abstract review. Critics including Steven Koonin and Roger Pielke Jr. point out that the 97% claim does NOT actually exclude named skeptics. Why?
questions.answer: The Cook criteria — 'humans contribute to warming' — are broad enough that named skeptics like Koonin and Lindzen would themselves count inside the 97%
choices: The Cook criteria — 'humans contribute to warming' — are broad enough that named skeptics like Koonin and Lindzen would themselves count inside the 97%
The Cook criteria explicitly excluded every skeptic by name — and the 97% measures unanimous agreement with the strongest IPCC catastrophe scenarios
The Cook study only polled members of one specific advocacy organization — and is openly understood to be unrepresentative of working scientists
The Cook study has been retracted by its journal — and is no longer cited by anyone in serious climate policy discussions
questions.context: Richard Lindzen (MIT atmospheric physics, IPCC AR3 author), Judith Curry (Georgia Tech climatology chair), Steven Koonin, Roy Spencer, John Christy and others accept that human activity contributes to warming. What they dispute is magnitude, feedbacks, model accuracy, and policy implications. The 97% statistic glides over those distinctions. The slogan does not refute the dissent it appears to refute.

questions.question: After John Cook's 2013 'consensus' study appeared, climate scientist David Legates and co-authors examined the same abstracts under Cook's own categorization system and published a 2015 response paper. What percentage of the 12,000 abstracts actually EXPLICITLY endorsed the strongest IPCC position — that humans cause the majority of warming?
questions.answer: Around 0.3% explicitly endorsed the strongest IPCC framing — well under 1%, not 97%, when the strongest claim is the one measured
choices: Around 0.3% explicitly endorsed the strongest IPCC framing — well under 1%, not 97%, when the strongest claim is the one measured
Around 97% explicitly endorsed the strongest IPCC framing — Legates's reanalysis fully confirmed the original Cook headline figure
Around 50% explicitly endorsed the strongest IPCC framing — Legates split the difference between Cook's claim and total skepticism
Around 88% explicitly endorsed the strongest IPCC framing — Legates found a modest reduction from Cook's number but still overwhelming agreement
questions.context: Legates et al. (2015) in *Science and Education* re-examined Cook's dataset using Cook's published criteria. Only 41 of 11,944 abstracts explicitly endorsed the strongest IPCC claim that humans cause most warming. The headline 97% combines weaker claims and abstracts that took no position. The bank teaches the kid to read past slogan statistics and ask what the underlying claim actually was.

questions.question: In November 2009, emails and files from the Climatic Research Unit at the University of East Anglia were leaked to the public — an event quickly nicknamed 'Climategate.' One email by CRU director Phil Jones used the phrase 'hide the decline' in reference to tree-ring data that diverged from instrumental temperature records after about 1960. What did the leaked correspondence actually reveal about how that data was handled?
questions.answer: Researchers privately discussed splicing instrumental data over tree-ring data where the proxies showed cooling — masking what would have undercut the iconic 'hockey stick' shape
choices: Researchers privately discussed splicing instrumental data over tree-ring data where the proxies showed cooling — masking what would have undercut the iconic 'hockey stick' shape
Researchers privately confirmed the hockey stick was based on flawless data — and the public release was a misunderstanding with no implications
Researchers privately discussed publishing every contrary data point even more prominently — exactly the opposite of what the leak suggested to readers
Researchers privately discovered an error and immediately retracted their entire body of work — in response to internal review by an independent panel
questions.context: Multiple official inquiries (House of Commons, Penn State, Muir Russell) cleared the researchers of scientific fraud per se, while noting they had been less than open with data and code requests. The phrase 'Mike's nature trick' (in a separate email) referred to Michael Mann's technique of splicing instrumental records onto proxy reconstructions in a 1998 *Nature* paper. The episode damaged public confidence in the field's openness — exactly when it could least afford to.

questions.question: Climategate emails from the Climatic Research Unit at East Anglia (released November 2009) included a line by Phil Jones: 'I've just completed Mike's Nature trick of adding in the real temps to each series for the last 20 years (i.e., from 1981 onwards) and from 1961 for Keith's to hide the decline.' What was the 'decline' being hidden?
questions.answer: Tree-ring proxy data showed cooling after about 1960, contradicting instrumental warming — researchers grafted the instrumental record onto the proxy to keep the graph rising
choices: Tree-ring proxy data showed cooling after about 1960, contradicting instrumental warming — researchers grafted the instrumental record onto the proxy to keep the graph rising
Tree-ring proxy data showed warming far beyond instrumental readings — researchers added the cooler instrumental data to moderate the alarming proxy results
Tree-ring proxy data showed perfect agreement with instruments — the 'trick' was simply a colloquial term for an excellent statistical match between the records
Tree-ring proxy data was never used in any climate reconstruction — the email was discussing geological core samples instead with no temperature implications
questions.context: The 'divergence problem' — that tree-ring proxies (which are used to reconstruct pre-instrumental temperatures back centuries) failed to track instrumental warming after ~1960 — is real and openly discussed in the technical literature. The Climategate concern was specifically about presentation: the WMO 1999 cover graph used the spliced record without disclosing the splice. Whether that constitutes fraud or merely poor presentation has been debated; the inquiries leaned toward the latter.

questions.question: After the Climategate emails leaked in November 2009, several official inquiries examined the conduct of the Climatic Research Unit researchers — including a UK Parliamentary committee, the Penn State inquiry into Michael Mann, and the Muir Russell independent review commissioned by UEA. Critics have noted a pattern across these inquiries. What did the investigations conclude, and what did skeptics say about the conclusions?
questions.answer: Inquiries cleared researchers of scientific fraud but found openness lapses — critics argued the panels did not interview key skeptics and reached conclusions limited to fraud while leaving the underlying data-handling concerns intact
choices: Inquiries cleared researchers of scientific fraud but found openness lapses — critics argued the panels did not interview key skeptics and reached conclusions limited to fraud while leaving the underlying data-handling concerns intact
Inquiries unanimously found the researchers guilty of every accusation — and resulted in immediate criminal prosecution in multiple jurisdictions worldwide
Inquiries refused to examine the leaked materials at all — and no official body ever issued any finding about the East Anglia correspondence
Inquiries definitively closed every question raised by the leaks — and critics universally agreed the investigations had been thorough and impartial
questions.context: The House of Commons Science and Technology Committee, the Penn State University inquiries (which examined Michael Mann), and the Muir Russell independent panel were the major inquiries. They generally cleared the researchers of fraud while flagging poor data-sharing practice and lack of openness. Steve McIntyre and Ross McKitrick, who had raised the original Hockey Stick critique, argued the inquiries did not seriously engage with the substantive methodological critiques. The kid's takeaway: 'cleared by inquiry' is not always the end of the story.

questions.question: Carbon-tax advocates promise their preferred policy will reduce global CO2 emissions. Critics of carbon taxes — including economists like Tyler Cowen, Bjorn Lomborg, and many others — point to a basic empirical observation about countries that have actually implemented carbon taxes versus countries that haven't. What does the evidence show?
questions.answer: Countries that implement carbon taxes export their emissions to non-taxing countries — global emissions are not reduced, only relocated, while the taxing country's industry weakens
choices: Countries that implement carbon taxes export their emissions to non-taxing countries — global emissions are not reduced, only relocated, while the taxing country's industry weakens
Countries that implement carbon taxes always achieve dramatic immediate global emission reductions — far in excess of what models predict in advance of the policy
Countries that implement carbon taxes have identical emission profiles to non-taxing countries — the tax has no effect on industrial behavior in any direction
Countries that implement carbon taxes have no industrial activity left to compare — every business immediately closes within months of any tax introduction
questions.context: Carbon leakage — emissions migrating to jurisdictions with weaker regulations — is documented in EU-ETS, Australia's brief 2012-14 carbon tax, and Canada's federal scheme. China, India, and other major emitters continue building coal capacity regardless. Critics argue the tax is wealth extraction dressed as climate policy: it raises revenue, hits working-class household budgets disproportionately (energy is a larger share of poor families' spending), and doesn't reduce planet-wide emissions.

questions.question: Carbon taxes raise the cost of energy — fuel, heating, electricity. Critics argue carbon taxes are regressive in effect even if they appear neutral on paper. Why do carbon taxes disproportionately burden working-class households?
questions.answer: Energy is a much larger share of low-income household spending than high-income — so any tax on energy hits poor families harder than rich, regardless of nominal rate equality
choices: Energy is a much larger share of low-income household spending than high-income — so any tax on energy hits poor families harder than rich, regardless of nominal rate equality
Energy is a much larger share of high-income household spending than low-income — so any tax on energy hits wealthy families harder than working class
Energy is an equal share of household spending across all income levels — so any tax on energy hits every household identically with no distributional effect at all
Energy is not actually taxed by carbon taxes at all — the tax falls only on industrial producers and never reaches household budgets in any form
questions.context: Heating, driving, and electricity together can run 20-30% of household budgets for low-income families versus single digits for the affluent. France's 2018 Yellow Vest protests were triggered by a fuel-tax increase explicitly justified on climate grounds. Various 'carbon dividend' schemes attempt to rebate the tax back to households, but the political dynamic remains: the tax visibly hits paychecks while the climate benefit (if any) is global and distant.

questions.question: Climate alarmism — distinct from the underlying scientific question of warming — has been analyzed by critics including Mike Hulme (King's College London), Roger Pielke Jr., and Bjorn Lomborg as displaying features more typical of religious apocalypticism than scientific inquiry. What feature of climate alarmism most clearly fits the apocalyptic pattern rather than the scientific?
questions.answer: Specific predicted dates for catastrophe quietly expire and are replaced with new dates — without acknowledgement, retraction, or update to the underlying confidence
choices: Specific predicted dates for catastrophe quietly expire and are replaced with new dates — without acknowledgement, retraction, or update to the underlying confidence
Specific predicted dates for catastrophe always arrive exactly as forecast — and the field publicly celebrates the accuracy of every previous projection
Specific predicted dates for catastrophe are never made by alarmist commentary — every claim is hedged with precise uncertainty bounds and timeframes
Specific predicted dates for catastrophe are randomly chosen — and the field acknowledges that the dates have no relationship to underlying physical models
questions.context: Mike Hulme's *Why We Disagree About Climate Change* (2009) explicitly treats the cultural-religious dimensions of climate discourse as worth naming. The pattern — failed prophecy followed by adjusted prophecy without epistemic update — is the move Leon Festinger documented in *When Prophecy Fails* (1956) about the Seekers UFO cult. Sincere belief plus motivated reasoning plus social pressure produces this signature even when the underlying science of warming is real.

questions.question: Climate alarmism in the 2010s and 2020s has involved adult activists directing moral demands AT children — and amplifying children's voices back at adult audiences as moral authority. Critics including psychologist Jordan Peterson and journalist Brendan O'Neill have called this pattern morally inverted. Why do critics describe this dynamic as a misuse of children?
questions.answer: Adults using children as moral mouthpieces shifts adult arguments behind a shield that adults cannot be argued against — and outsources adult anxiety to kids who lack the context to refuse
choices: Adults using children as moral mouthpieces shifts adult arguments behind a shield that adults cannot be argued against — and outsources adult anxiety to kids who lack the context to refuse
Adults using children as moral mouthpieces is widely celebrated by every critic — as the most accurate possible way to evaluate scientific claims about future risk
Adults using children as moral mouthpieces only happens in fictional novels — no actual climate activism has ever featured children in any speaking role at all
Adults using children as moral mouthpieces is mandated by international scientific bodies — and refusing to do so is treated as professional misconduct
questions.context: Greta Thunberg's 2019 UN speech ('How dare you...') was widely amplified by adult institutions including the UN itself. Children striking school for climate gained official cover from adult organizations including teachers' unions in Europe. Surveys (Hickman et al. 2021 in *Lancet Planetary Health*) found 56% of young people felt 'humanity is doomed' — a level of despair generated, in part, by adult catastrophist messaging directed at them.

questions.question: Climate alarmism produces a recurring observable pattern that critics — Alex Epstein, Bjorn Lomborg, Michael Shellenberger — repeatedly name. The pattern shows up most visibly at gatherings like the World Economic Forum at Davos, where attendees publicly demand sacrifice from working-class populations while flying private jets to those same gatherings. What does the pattern reveal about the rhetoric?
questions.answer: The rhetoric functions as moralism aimed downward — sacrifice demanded from those without private jets, while the elites issuing the demands exempt themselves from any of it
choices: The rhetoric functions as moralism aimed downward — sacrifice demanded from those without private jets, while the elites issuing the demands exempt themselves from any of it
The rhetoric is applied uniformly — Davos attendees travel only by bicycle and walk to every conference venue in matching reusable shoes
The rhetoric is purely scientific — and the private-jet pattern at Davos is a fabrication invented by political opponents with no airport records
The rhetoric is exclusively about the wealthy — and working-class populations are explicitly told their behavior is irrelevant to outcomes
questions.context: Records from Zurich and Geneva airports each Davos week document hundreds of private-jet arrivals. The same dynamic plays out at COP climate conferences. Critics argue that whatever the underlying science, the political deployment of climate rhetoric functions as a moralism that disciplines working-class life — cars, beef, gas heating, foreign holidays — while exempting the donor-class life of the people doing the moralizing.

questions.question: About 50 million years ago, during the Eocene epoch, Earth was dramatically warmer than today — palm trees grew in Wyoming, crocodile-like reptiles lived in the Canadian Arctic, and Antarctica was forested. Atmospheric CO2 levels are estimated at 1000+ ppm versus today's ~420 ppm. What does the Eocene establish about modern climate alarm framing?
questions.answer: Earth's climate has been radically warmer than the present long before any industrial CO2 — and life flourished, not collapsed, in those warmer states
choices: Earth's climate has been radically warmer than the present long before any industrial CO2 — and life flourished, not collapsed, in those warmer states
Earth's climate has never been meaningfully warmer than today — and the Eocene fossils were misdated by paleontologists in unrelated work
Earth's climate during the Eocene was cooler than today — and the palm-tree fossils in Wyoming are misidentified pinecones from a much later period
Earth's climate during the Eocene was identical to today — and the cooler arctic regions today are an artifact of recent measurement errors
questions.context: Eocene fossil sites — the Green River Formation, Ellesmere Island in Canada, Antarctic Peninsula fossil flora — document a planet far hotter than today's. Life thrived, with mammalian, reptilian, and floral diversity now associated with the tropics existing at high latitudes. This does NOT mean modern warming is benign or has no consequences — it does mean the framing 'warmer climates are existentially unsurvivable for life' is contradicted by Earth's own deep record.

questions.question: Between roughly 950 and 1250 AD, the North Atlantic region experienced a warm interval now called the Medieval Warm Period (MWP) or Medieval Climate Anomaly. Vikings farmed Greenland; England grew grapes; Iceland was settled. Michael Mann's 1998 'hockey stick' graph famously flattened this period out — sparking decades of debate. Why does the MWP matter for the modern climate discussion?
questions.answer: It documents pre-industrial warm intervals without modern CO2 — so attributing all modern warmth to CO2 alone requires explaining how the same range happened earlier without it
choices: It documents pre-industrial warm intervals without modern CO2 — so attributing all modern warmth to CO2 alone requires explaining how the same range happened earlier without it
It documents pre-industrial cool intervals — and modern warmth is the first warm period in Earth's history without any earlier comparable case at all
It documents pre-industrial extreme cold — Viking settlements in Greenland survived only because the climate was much colder than today
It documents pre-industrial extreme weather only — there is no temperature signal in any record from the medieval period in any region of Earth
questions.context: The MWP is most clearly documented in North Atlantic proxies, but evidence for global extent is mixed — some regions show clear warmth (Europe, Iceland, Greenland), others less so. The Hockey Stick controversy (Mann 1998, McKitrick-McIntyre 2003 critique, IPCC AR3 cover graph) revolved partly around whether the MWP was global or regional. The kid's point: pre-industrial natural variability happens, and modern attribution claims have to live with that.

questions.question: Between roughly 1300 and 1850 AD, the Northern Hemisphere experienced a notably colder interval called the Little Ice Age (LIA). The Thames froze hard enough for ice fairs; Dutch canals froze regularly (immortalized in Dutch paintings); the Norse Greenland colony collapsed. The LIA ended around 1850 — which happens to be roughly when modern instrument records begin. Why does that timing matter for evaluating modern warming?
questions.answer: Modern instrument records begin near the COLDEST point of recent millennia — so any subsequent warming will look more dramatic than if records had started in a normal interval
choices: Modern instrument records begin near the COLDEST point of recent millennia — so any subsequent warming will look more dramatic than if records had started in a normal interval
Modern instrument records begin during the WARMEST point of recent millennia — so any subsequent warming should appear muted, not amplified
Modern instrument records begin at a perfectly typical temperature — so the LIA has no implication for how subsequent records appear today
Modern instrument records did not actually begin in 1850 — they began in 1750, well before the LIA had ended in any northern region
questions.context: Frozen Thames ice fairs (1607-1814), Dutch winter-landscape paintings (Avercamp, Bruegel), collapse of the Norse Greenland colony (~1450) all document the LIA. The 'baseline' from which modern warming is measured matters a lot. Koonin emphasizes this point: 'warming since 1850' is real, but 1850 is not a neutral starting point — it is a cold trough. The framing affects how alarming a given trend appears.

questions.question: Between about 8000 and 4000 years ago — well into the Holocene, the warm interglacial we still live in — temperatures across much of the Northern Hemisphere are believed to have been somewhat warmer than today. This interval is called the Holocene Climatic Optimum or Mid-Holocene Warm Period. What is the recognition for a kid reading 'unprecedented warmth' claims about the modern era?
questions.answer: The current Holocene interglacial has been warmer than today within human history — modern warmth is not unprecedented even within the most recent geological epoch
choices: The current Holocene interglacial has been warmer than today within human history — modern warmth is not unprecedented even within the most recent geological epoch
The current Holocene interglacial has been continuously cooler than today — modern warmth is the warmest moment in the entire 10,000-year period
The current Holocene interglacial does not exist — geologists no longer use the term and there has been no warm interval since the last ice age
The current Holocene interglacial began only 200 years ago — and modern warmth coincides with the very first warming since deep prehistoric times
questions.context: Greenland ice cores (GISP2, NGRIP) and global proxy syntheses indicate the early-to-mid Holocene was likely 1-2°C warmer than today in many high-latitude regions. Sahara was greener; treelines were higher; alpine glaciers smaller. This does NOT mean human-caused warming is benign — it means the framing 'unprecedented in Earth's history' is not technically accurate even on the scale of the current epoch.

questions.question: Between roughly 1645 and 1715, sunspot counts collapsed to near zero — a period now called the Maunder Minimum. This stretch coincided with the deepest cold of the Little Ice Age in Europe: frozen Thames ice fairs, severe winters, crop failures contributing to famines. What does the Maunder Minimum suggest about climate drivers?
questions.answer: Solar variability appears to drive significant climate change on multi-decade timescales — independent of CO2, which was not industrially elevated in the 17th century
choices: Solar variability appears to drive significant climate change on multi-decade timescales — independent of CO2, which was not industrially elevated in the 17th century
Solar variability has no detectable effect on Earth's climate — the Maunder Minimum and the Little Ice Age are entirely unrelated coincidences
Solar variability is the ONLY driver of climate change — and CO2 has no effect of any kind on temperature in any era of Earth's history
Solar variability and CO2 always move together — so it is impossible to disentangle their effects in any historical period at all
questions.context: The Maunder Minimum (named for English astronomer Edward Walter Maunder) and the Dalton Minimum (1790-1830) are two well-documented solar-output low intervals. Sunspot records (Hevelius, Cassini, Galileo) document the Maunder collapse. Total solar irradiance variation during the cycle is modest (~0.1%), but indirect amplification through UV-stratosphere-circulation effects (Lockwood, Solanki) may make the climate response larger than the irradiance change alone would predict.

questions.question: Earth's orbit changes slowly over tens of thousands of years — eccentricity (about 100,000-year cycle), obliquity (the tilt of the axis, about 41,000-year cycle), and precession (about 26,000-year cycle). Serbian mathematician Milutin Milanković worked out the math while interned during WWI. What's the empirical match between these orbital cycles and Earth's climate history?
questions.answer: Ice-age cycles over the last 800,000 years closely track the orbital cycles — Milanković's prediction was vindicated by deep-sea sediment cores in the 1970s
choices: Ice-age cycles over the last 800,000 years closely track the orbital cycles — Milanković's prediction was vindicated by deep-sea sediment cores in the 1970s
Ice-age cycles over the last 800,000 years show no relationship to orbital cycles — and Milanković's hypothesis has been definitively refuted
Ice-age cycles over the last 800,000 years happen at random — and no astronomical or terrestrial driver of any kind has been identified
Ice-age cycles over the last 800,000 years are driven entirely by human activity — and Milanković's orbital calculations are irrelevant to climate
questions.context: The Hays, Imbrie, Shackleton 1976 paper in *Science* — 'Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages' — used deep-sea sediment oxygen-isotope ratios to confirm Milanković's prediction that ice-age cycles match orbital geometry. The basic explanation for why Earth has had ice ages at all over the last 2-3 million years rests on orbital forcing. Modern climate cannot be discussed honestly without this background.

questions.question: Cities are systematically hotter than surrounding rural areas — asphalt, concrete, building density, waste heat from air conditioners and cars all warm the local environment. This is the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. Surface temperature stations are disproportionately located in or near urban areas. What does this mean for the global temperature record?
questions.answer: Some fraction of measured 'global warming' likely reflects expansion of urban areas around stations — an effect that must be subtracted from the raw record but is contested in size
choices: Some fraction of measured 'global warming' likely reflects expansion of urban areas around stations — an effect that must be subtracted from the raw record but is contested in size
Some fraction of measured 'global warming' is entirely the urban heat island — and there has been no real warming of any kind outside city limits at any time
Some fraction of measured 'global warming' would exist regardless of station location — the urban heat island effect has been ruled to be exactly zero
Some fraction of measured 'global warming' is hidden — the urban heat island effect is so large that real warming is actually three times higher than reported
questions.context: Roger Pielke Sr. and Anthony Watts have documented poor station siting (the 'Surface Stations' project: 89% of US Climate Reference Network stations failed siting standards in early audits). NOAA/NASA make UHI 'homogenization' adjustments. The size of the residual UHI contamination after adjustment is the contested point. None of this refutes warming as a phenomenon — but it does qualify how confidently the magnitude can be stated.

questions.question: Modern global temperature records (GISS, NOAA, HadCRUT, BEST) require many adjustments — for station moves, instrument changes, time-of-observation differences, and urban heat island contamination. Critics have documented a recurring pattern in those adjustments: published past temperatures tend to drift downward over successive revisions, while present temperatures stay or drift upward. What does this pattern look like in net effect?
questions.answer: The cumulative effect of adjustments is to cool the past and warm the present — increasing the apparent warming trend over what raw data alone would show
choices: The cumulative effect of adjustments is to cool the past and warm the present — increasing the apparent warming trend over what raw data alone would show
The cumulative effect of adjustments is to warm the past and cool the present — reducing the apparent warming trend below what raw data shows
The cumulative effect of adjustments is exactly zero — and raw data and adjusted data show identical warming trends in every published record
The cumulative effect of adjustments is to reduce uncertainty — and the published record reflects no net change in the trend after adjustment
questions.context: Tony Heller, Steve McIntyre, and others have documented specific revisions where past values drifted cooler while present values stayed or drifted warmer between dataset versions (e.g., GISS revisions of 1934 vs 1998). NOAA defenders argue every individual adjustment has documented physical justification (instrument changes, station relocations). The contested question is whether the pattern of adjustments is biased or merely the product of legitimate corrections — and whether the resulting trend is therefore over- or under-stated.

questions.question: When researchers separate temperature stations into rural versus urban subsets, the resulting trends differ. Critics including Anthony Watts (Surface Stations project) and Ross McKitrick have argued the rural-only trend is systematically smaller than the urban-influenced trend that dominates published records. What's the recognition skill the kid needs reading 'hottest year on record' headlines?
questions.answer: The 'record' depends on adjustment choices, station coverage, and reference baseline — claimed records differ across datasets and depend on methodology, not just thermometer readings
choices: The 'record' depends on adjustment choices, station coverage, and reference baseline — claimed records differ across datasets and depend on methodology, not just thermometer readings
The 'record' is read directly from a single global thermometer — and no adjustments or methodological choices are ever involved in any temperature claim
The 'record' is identical across all published datasets — every method gives exactly the same number with no detectable disagreement at all
The 'record' is purely a satellite measurement now — and surface station data has been completely abandoned by every research group worldwide
questions.context: Different temperature reconstructions disagree by tenths of a degree on which years are 'warmest.' UAH satellite (Spencer, Christy) typically shows smaller warming than surface records. The Berkeley Earth (BEST) project led by Richard Muller — originally a skeptic — confirmed warming but did not resolve the magnitude debate. The kid's skill: read the methodology section, not just the headline.

questions.question: In 1968 Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich published *The Population Bomb*, predicting that 'in the 1970s the world will undergo famines — hundreds of millions of people are going to starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now.' What actually happened to global hunger between 1970 and 2020?
questions.answer: Starvation rates plummeted — the global hunger rate fell from about 1 in 3 in 1970 to under 1 in 10 by the mid-2010s, the opposite of Ehrlich's prediction
choices: Starvation rates plummeted — the global hunger rate fell from about 1 in 3 in 1970 to under 1 in 10 by the mid-2010s, the opposite of Ehrlich's prediction
Starvation rates rose dramatically — global famines killed hundreds of millions in the 1970s exactly as Ehrlich had forecast
Starvation rates stayed identical — Ehrlich's prediction was neither confirmed nor refuted across the half century after publication
Starvation rates became immeasurable — global statistics ceased being collected in the 1970s and no comparison is possible
questions.context: Norman Borlaug's Green Revolution dwarf wheat (Nobel Peace 1970), Hans Rosling's data work, and World Bank figures all document the collapse in absolute hunger between 1970 and 2020. Ehrlich never retracted; he received the Crafoord Prize in 1990, the same year his predictions had clearly failed. His career arc is a striking case of how prestige and prediction-failure can coexist with no professional cost.

questions.question: In 1980 economist Julian Simon publicly challenged biologist Paul Ehrlich to a wager. Ehrlich was to choose any five raw materials he expected to become scarcer (and therefore more expensive) over the next decade. Simon bet the opposite. Ehrlich picked chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten. When 1990 arrived, what was the verdict?
questions.answer: Simon won — the prices of all five metals had FALLEN even as global population grew by 800 million people, refuting the scarcity prediction outright
choices: Simon won — the prices of all five metals had FALLEN even as global population grew by 800 million people, refuting the scarcity prediction outright
Ehrlich won — every metal he picked had skyrocketed in price exactly as he predicted, vindicating limits-to-growth catastrophism
The wager was declared a draw — three metals rose and two fell, with no clear winner determinable from market prices
The wager was never resolved — both parties agreed to cancel the bet before the 1990 deadline arrived and no payment changed hands
questions.context: Simon's argument: human ingenuity finds substitutes, recycling, and efficient extraction faster than population grows; resources are not fixed because human creativity is the ultimate resource. Ehrlich paid out $576.07 (the inflation-adjusted price difference) in October 1990. He proposed a second wager on different metrics; Simon declined to define forward-looking trends as resources. The lesson: limits-to-growth catastrophism has a documented failure record.

questions.question: In 1972 the Club of Rome published *The Limits to Growth* — a Meadows-Randers-Behrens computer-simulation forecast warning that under business-as-usual growth, gold would be depleted by 1981, mercury by 1985, tin by 1987, oil by 1992, copper by 1993, natural gas by 1993, and silver by 1985. What is the recognition skill the kid needs to learn from *Limits to Growth*?
questions.answer: Computer-model catastrophe forecasts can be confidently wrong about specific dated outcomes — and persisting confidence in updated forecasts despite past failures is itself a warning sign
choices: Computer-model catastrophe forecasts can be confidently wrong about specific dated outcomes — and persisting confidence in updated forecasts despite past failures is itself a warning sign
Computer-model catastrophe forecasts always confirm their original predictions exactly — and the resources predicted to deplete in *Limits to Growth* did vanish on the predicted timelines
Computer-model catastrophe forecasts are never tested — and there is no way to know whether *Limits to Growth* predicted accurately or not after publication
Computer-model catastrophe forecasts ceased being made after *Limits to Growth* — and no modeled prediction has been published since 1972 on any topic
questions.context: *Limits to Growth* (Meadows et al., 1972) sold 30 million copies. The depletion timetables were embarrassingly wrong — by 2020, none of the named resources had run out; many had become cheaper. The book was followed by 'updates' (1992, 2004) that did not concede the past failures but issued new dates. The pattern of failed forecast followed by undeterred new forecast is the kid's recognition target.

questions.question: Multiple high-profile predictions in the 2000s and 2010s forecast an ice-free summer Arctic Ocean by specific dates: Al Gore (2007, '5-7 years'); BBC reporting NSIDC researchers (2008, 'by 2013'); Peter Wadhams of Cambridge (2012, 'by 2015 or 2016'); various IPCC reports (2007, 'by 2030 plausible'). What is the actual September Arctic sea-ice trend?
questions.answer: September ice extent has declined since 1979 but has not reached zero — multiple specific predicted years passed with ice still present, while the trend itself continues
choices: September ice extent has declined since 1979 but has not reached zero — multiple specific predicted years passed with ice still present, while the trend itself continues
September ice extent has reached zero exactly as every prediction forecast — and the Arctic Ocean has been ice-free every summer since 2013
September ice extent has grown rapidly since 1979 — and there is no detectable downward trend of any kind in the satellite record
September ice extent has stayed exactly stable since 1979 — there is neither warming nor cooling in any Arctic record
questions.context: Satellite-era Arctic September ice extent has trended downward since 1979, with a minimum of ~3.4 million km² in 2012. As of the mid-2020s, ice still forms each winter and substantial ice remains each summer minimum. The trend is real but the dramatic predictions of specific zero-ice years all failed. Koonin's *Unsettled* highlights this pattern: trend is one thing, dated catastrophe predictions are another, and the second has a documented failure record.

questions.question: In 2016 a research team led by Zaichun Zhu published in *Nature Climate Change* a satellite-based analysis of vegetation cover change since the early 1980s. They examined what global plant life had actually done over three decades of rising CO2. What did the satellite data show?
questions.answer: Earth has measurably greened since 1980 — an area roughly twice the size of the continental US has gained vegetation, driven significantly by CO2 fertilization
choices: Earth has measurably greened since 1980 — an area roughly twice the size of the continental US has gained vegetation, driven significantly by CO2 fertilization
Earth has measurably browned since 1980 — virtually all plant cover has collapsed across continents in line with catastrophist warnings
Earth has stayed exactly the same since 1980 — satellite data show no detectable change in any direction over the entire period
Earth has not been measured since 1980 — no satellite observations of vegetation cover have ever been published in any journal
questions.context: Zhu et al. attribute about 70% of greening to CO2 fertilization, with the rest from nitrogen deposition, climate change, and land-use changes. Plants use CO2 in photosynthesis; more CO2 means many plants grow faster with less water (improved water-use efficiency). The greening is not a refutation of climate concern as such — but it is a real benefit that public coverage rarely mentions, since it complicates the pure-cost framing of CO2.

questions.question: Commercial greenhouses routinely pump CO2 levels up to 1000-1500 ppm to boost crop yields — vegetable, flower, and cannabis growers all do this. The mechanism is well established. What physiological effect does elevated CO2 have on most plants?
questions.answer: Plants photosynthesize faster and use water more efficiently — closing stomata more, losing less water, and producing more biomass per unit of input
choices: Plants photosynthesize faster and use water more efficiently — closing stomata more, losing less water, and producing more biomass per unit of input
Plants photosynthesize more slowly at high CO2 — and commercial greenhouses pump CO2 only to harm crop growth as a poorly-understood industrial practice
Plants have no measurable response to CO2 at any level — and greenhouse CO2 enrichment is universally understood to be a waste of money
Plants die immediately when CO2 exceeds 400 ppm — and greenhouses operate below atmospheric levels to keep crops alive at all
questions.context: Atmospheric CO2 was about 280 ppm pre-industrial, around 420 ppm today, and 1000-1500 ppm in commercial greenhouses. The C3 photosynthesis pathway (most plants including wheat, rice, soybeans) is CO2-limited at current atmospheric levels. Crop yields under CO2 enrichment can rise 20-30% for major staples. This is real, well-documented agricultural science — and it puts a real-world benefit on the other side of the cost-only framing.

questions.question: Earth's atmospheric CO2 has varied dramatically over geological time. During the Cambrian explosion of complex life (~540 million years ago), CO2 levels are estimated at roughly 4000-7000 ppm — over ten times today's level. During much of the Mesozoic (dinosaur era), CO2 was likely 1000-2000+ ppm. What does this geological history establish?
questions.answer: CO2 has been radically higher than today during periods when life flourished and diversified — meaning the framing 'high CO2 means dead biosphere' is not supported by Earth's deep record
choices: CO2 has been radically higher than today during periods when life flourished and diversified — meaning the framing 'high CO2 means dead biosphere' is not supported by Earth's deep record
CO2 has never exceeded 420 ppm at any point in Earth's history — and the modern level is unprecedented in the entire geological record
CO2 has only existed in the atmosphere since the Industrial Revolution — and there were no measurable levels of any kind before 1800
CO2 has always varied by less than 10 ppm over Earth's history — and the modern variation is several thousand times larger than any past change
questions.context: Proxies for ancient CO2 include carbon-isotope ratios in marine sediments, stomatal density in fossil leaves, and chemical equilibria in carbonate rocks. Reconstructions disagree on exact numbers but all show CO2 over Earth's deep history radically higher than today's. This does not refute concern about RATE of modern change — but it does qualify the 'CO2 itself means catastrophe' framing.

questions.question: In 1998 two independent supernova-survey teams — Saul Perlmutter's Supernova Cosmology Project and Brian Schmidt + Adam Riess's High-Z Supernova Search — published a finding that overturned a key assumption in cosmology. They had assumed cosmic expansion was DECELERATING under gravity's pull. What did the Type Ia supernova distance measurements actually show?
questions.answer: The expansion is ACCELERATING — distant supernovae are dimmer than they should be, meaning the universe is being pushed apart by an unknown force
choices: The expansion is ACCELERATING — distant supernovae are dimmer than they should be, meaning the universe is being pushed apart by an unknown force
The expansion is exactly steady — distant supernovae match the predictions of a static-universe model with no acceleration
The expansion is reversing — distant supernovae appear in the wrong direction and the universe is contracting toward a Big Crunch
The expansion never occurred — distant supernovae were misidentified and the universe has not changed size since the Big Bang
questions.context: Perlmutter, Schmidt, and Riess shared the 2011 Nobel in Physics. Type Ia supernovae are 'standard candles' — their intrinsic brightness is well-known, so apparent brightness gives distance. The data showed distant supernovae were 25% dimmer than expected — they were further away than a decelerating universe would predict. The unknown driver was named 'dark energy' and constitutes about 68% of the universe's energy content.

questions.question: If dark energy is identified with the cosmological constant — Einstein's lambda — quantum field theory makes a specific prediction about the vacuum-energy density that should fill empty space. When physicists compute that quantum prediction and compare it to the observed value of dark energy, the disagreement is famously stark. By roughly how many orders of magnitude does theory exceed observation?
questions.answer: About 120 orders of magnitude — the largest known disagreement between any theoretical prediction and any empirical observation in all of physics
choices: About 120 orders of magnitude — the largest known disagreement between any theoretical prediction and any empirical observation in all of physics
About 2 orders of magnitude — a small discrepancy that has now been fully resolved by recent measurements
About 6 orders of magnitude — a moderate disagreement comparable to other open problems in particle physics
About zero — theory and observation agree perfectly and the cosmological constant problem has been completely solved
questions.context: The cosmological-constant problem is sometimes called the worst theoretical prediction in physics. Quantum field theory predicts a vacuum energy that should curl up the observable universe; the observed dark-energy density is finite but tiny. Either the QFT calculation is profoundly wrong, or some unknown mechanism cancels the prediction to 120 decimal places exactly except for one tiny residual. Both possibilities are deeply uncomfortable, and neither has been resolved.

questions.question: Dark energy has been measured with increasing precision since its 1998 discovery — by supernova surveys, the cosmic microwave background (WMAP, Planck), baryon acoustic oscillations, and the Dark Energy Survey. But what dark energy actually IS, in physical terms, remains undetermined. Which of the following best characterizes the current state of knowledge?
questions.answer: We've measured its effects to within a few percent — but we have no detection of any particle or field that would explain WHAT it physically is
choices: We've measured its effects to within a few percent — but we have no detection of any particle or field that would explain WHAT it physically is
We've identified dark energy as a specific known elementary particle — confirmed by direct detection in collider experiments by the early 2020s
We've ruled out dark energy as an artifact of measurement — the observations have been retracted and the topic is no longer studied
We've replaced dark energy with normal matter — the original anomaly was resolved by simply counting more atoms in galaxies
questions.context: Candidate explanations include: the cosmological constant (a fixed property of space); quintessence (a slowly varying dynamical scalar field); modified gravity at large scales; selection-effect explanations from cosmic inhomogeneity. None has decisive empirical support. The DESI 2024 results hinted at possible time-evolution of dark energy beyond a fixed constant, which would rule out the simplest interpretation, but the result has not been confirmed.

questions.question: In April 2024 the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) collaboration released a first year of results from a multi-year survey mapping galaxies across cosmic distances. The results hinted at something physicists had not previously confirmed. What did the early DESI data suggest about dark energy?
questions.answer: Dark energy may not be a fixed cosmological constant — it may be evolving in strength over cosmic time, which would force a major revision of the standard model
choices: Dark energy may not be a fixed cosmological constant — it may be evolving in strength over cosmic time, which would force a major revision of the standard model
Dark energy is exactly a fixed cosmological constant — DESI confirmed the simplest possible interpretation with no hint of any further complexity
Dark energy does not exist — DESI showed the universe is actually decelerating and the 1998 discovery has now been overturned
Dark energy is identical to dark matter — DESI confirmed they are the same substance with two names by accident
questions.context: DESI is mapping ~40 million galaxies across the universe using a fiber-fed spectrograph at Kitt Peak. The first-year results showed possible deviation from the simplest cosmological-constant model (w = -1) at a few standard deviations. Confirmation requires more data, but if real, the result would be a major step toward understanding what dark energy actually IS. The mid-2020s remain an unresolved chapter — exactly the kind of open question the bank honors.

questions.question: Dark matter — first inferred from galaxy rotation curves (Vera Rubin's work in the 1970s) — has been hunted for decades with direct-detection experiments. Underground laboratories around the world host detectors like XENON, LUX-ZEPLIN, PandaX, and others, all searching for a recoil signal from a passing dark-matter particle. As of the mid-2020s, what have the direct-detection experiments found?
questions.answer: Nothing — every direct-detection experiment has returned null results, ruling out increasingly large regions of parameter space for the leading WIMP hypothesis
choices: Nothing — every direct-detection experiment has returned null results, ruling out increasingly large regions of parameter space for the leading WIMP hypothesis
Everything — every direct-detection experiment has confirmed WIMP dark matter with multiple independent detections by independent teams
Half — some experiments have detected WIMPs and others have not, with the disagreement still under active investigation by the field
Reversed — experiments have detected anti-dark-matter but not normal dark matter, requiring a new theoretical framework
questions.context: WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) were the favored dark-matter candidate for decades. XENON1T, LUX, PandaX-4T, LZ have pushed sensitivity limits down by factors of millions over twenty years. No conclusive detection. Alternative candidates — axions, sterile neutrinos, primordial black holes, modified gravity (MOND) — are receiving more attention. The honest answer about dark matter's identity in the mid-2020s: we still don't know what it IS.

questions.question: In the 1970s astronomer Vera Rubin used spectroscopic measurements at Lowell and Kitt Peak observatories to map how stars orbit at different radii inside galaxies. Newtonian gravity predicts that outer stars should orbit slower than inner ones — the way outer planets in the solar system orbit slower than inner ones. What did Rubin's measurements actually show?
questions.answer: Outer stars orbit just as fast as inner ones — meaning the gravitational mass extends far beyond visible matter, requiring something invisible to hold the galaxies together
choices: Outer stars orbit just as fast as inner ones — meaning the gravitational mass extends far beyond visible matter, requiring something invisible to hold the galaxies together
Outer stars orbit much slower than inner ones — fully consistent with Newtonian gravity and visible matter alone with no anomaly at all
Outer stars do not orbit galactic centers — Rubin's measurements showed random motion with no detectable gravitational binding
Outer stars orbit backward — Rubin's measurements showed the galaxies are rotating in the opposite direction of inner regions
questions.context: Rubin's flat rotation curves are foundational evidence for dark matter. She and her collaborator Kent Ford measured galaxy after galaxy and found the same anomaly. Modern observations confirm it across thousands of galaxies. Either there is additional invisible mass (the dark-matter explanation) or gravity itself differs from Newton/Einstein at galactic scales (the MOND alternative, proposed by Mordehai Milgrom). Both options remain on the table.

questions.question: An alternative to dark matter — Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) — was proposed in 1983 by Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom. Rather than adding invisible mass, MOND modifies gravity at low accelerations, producing the observed flat rotation curves without dark matter. What is MOND's current status in physics?
questions.answer: MOND explains galaxy-scale phenomena impressively but struggles with cluster-scale and cosmological observations — it remains a minority but live alternative
choices: MOND explains galaxy-scale phenomena impressively but struggles with cluster-scale and cosmological observations — it remains a minority but live alternative
MOND has been definitively falsified at every scale — and no physicist publishes work in the framework anymore as of the 2010s
MOND has replaced dark matter as the consensus explanation — and direct-detection experiments are no longer funded by any government
MOND has never been published in any physics journal — and the framework exists only in popular books for non-specialist audiences
questions.context: MOND's strongest case is the Tully-Fisher relation and the consistency of galaxy rotation curves across many systems. Its main difficulties are the Bullet Cluster (where dark-matter and visible matter appear separated by collision dynamics), CMB acoustic peaks, and structure formation. Stacy McGaugh, Bob Sanders, and others continue active MOND research. The mid-2020s remain genuinely open between dark-matter and modified-gravity explanations.

questions.question: The James Webb Space Telescope launched December 25, 2021, and began returning science in mid-2022. One early surprise was its discovery of large, mature-looking galaxies at very high redshift — meaning these galaxies existed when the universe was only a few hundred million years old. What was unexpected about these JWST findings?
questions.answer: The galaxies appeared larger and more mature than standard cosmological models predict — challenging the timeline of how quickly galaxies could have formed and grown
choices: The galaxies appeared larger and more mature than standard cosmological models predict — challenging the timeline of how quickly galaxies could have formed and grown
The galaxies appeared exactly as predicted — JWST observations precisely confirmed every standard-model expectation with no anomaly
The galaxies were invisible at high redshift — JWST detected no early galaxies of any kind despite its enhanced sensitivity
The galaxies were not galaxies at all — they were misidentified telescope artifacts that were quickly retracted by NASA
questions.context: Papers including Labbé et al. 2023 in *Nature* reported 'extremely massive' galaxies at z ~ 7-9 (about 500-700 million years after the Big Bang) — sometimes called 'too big to exist' under standard LambdaCDM. Subsequent analysis softened the claims somewhat (some objects were AGN, mass estimates have uncertainties), but the pattern of 'earlier and more mature than expected' has held. The standard model is being tested, not just confirmed.

questions.question: JWST's findings of large, mature-looking galaxies at very high redshift — sometimes characterized as 'too big to exist' under the standard LambdaCDM cosmological model — have been discussed at varying levels of alarm by the field. What is the honest scientific framing of where things stand?
questions.answer: Some observations strain the standard model but do not yet falsify it — uncertainties in mass estimates and possible alternative models leave the situation genuinely open
choices: Some observations strain the standard model but do not yet falsify it — uncertainties in mass estimates and possible alternative models leave the situation genuinely open
Every observation confirms the standard model exactly — there is no remaining tension between JWST data and prior cosmological expectations
Every observation refutes the standard model completely — cosmology has been overthrown and the Big Bang is now rejected by working researchers
Every observation has been retracted — JWST data has been ruled to be inadmissible by the relevant scientific bodies
questions.context: Major papers in *Nature*, *ApJ*, and other journals have raised questions about how rapidly large galaxies could have formed. Reassessments have moderated some of the most alarming claims, but tensions remain. Some have invoked early massive black holes, primordial seed galaxies, modified initial conditions, or alternative cosmological frameworks. The kid's point: the standard model is a working framework, not a closed answer — and JWST is providing the kind of data that tests it.

questions.question: Physicists Steven Weinberg in 1989 wrote an influential review of what he called the cosmological-constant problem. The problem is that quantum field theory's prediction for the vacuum energy of empty space is enormously larger than the value of dark energy actually observed in the universe. How does Weinberg's review describe the status of the problem?
questions.answer: It is one of the most embarrassing failures of theoretical physics — a mismatch so vast that any 'natural' explanation seems impossible without invoking new physics or fine-tuning
choices: It is one of the most embarrassing failures of theoretical physics — a mismatch so vast that any 'natural' explanation seems impossible without invoking new physics or fine-tuning
It is fully solved within the standard model — Weinberg's review confirmed that no remaining problem exists in any direction
It is a minor numerical disagreement — the observed and predicted values differ by less than a factor of two and the issue is essentially closed
It is not actually a problem at all — Weinberg's review concluded that the apparent disagreement reflects only measurement error
questions.context: Steven Weinberg, who won the 1979 Nobel for electroweak unification, treated the cosmological-constant problem with the seriousness it deserved. His 1989 review in *Reviews of Modern Physics* set the terms for the discussion. Decades later, the problem remains unsolved. The disagreement between theory and observation is so vast that it suggests something fundamental is missing in our understanding of either gravity or quantum field theory or both.

questions.question: Some physicists — including Andrei Linde, Alan Guth, and Sean Carroll — argue that the cosmological-constant problem and other fine-tuning puzzles may be explained by a multiverse: a vast ensemble of regions or worlds with different physical constants, of which we naturally inhabit one with constants compatible with life. Critics including Paul Davies, Peter Woit, and Sabine Hossenfelder name a structural concern with multiverse explanations. What is it?
questions.answer: Multiverse hypotheses generally cannot be empirically tested — they explain why our universe has the constants it has by invoking unobservable other universes
choices: Multiverse hypotheses generally cannot be empirically tested — they explain why our universe has the constants it has by invoking unobservable other universes
Multiverse hypotheses have all been definitively confirmed — by direct observation of other universes through dedicated telescope facilities
Multiverse hypotheses have all been definitively refuted — by the absence of observable signals from outside our local cosmic neighborhood
Multiverse hypotheses have all been retracted by their original proponents — and no living physicist still works on the framework
questions.context: Multiverse frameworks include eternal inflation (Linde, Guth, Vilenkin), the string landscape (Susskind), and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics. They are deeply discussed in modern physics — but their critics, including Hossenfelder in *Lost in Math* (2018) and Woit in *Not Even Wrong* (2006), argue they exit the empirical-falsifiability paradigm that has defined physics. The debate is alive: are we expanding science, or weakening it?

questions.question: The anthropic principle — articulated by Brandon Carter in 1973 and developed by John Barrow and Frank Tipler — observes that the physical constants of our universe appear remarkably fine-tuned to permit complex chemistry and therefore life. Carl Sagan and many others have noted that small changes in the fine-structure constant, cosmological constant, or proton-electron mass ratio would preclude life. How do critics characterize the anthropic principle as an EXPLANATION?
questions.answer: It restates the observation that we exist — but provides no causal mechanism for why constants take the values they do, leaving the puzzle structurally intact
choices: It restates the observation that we exist — but provides no causal mechanism for why constants take the values they do, leaving the puzzle structurally intact
It provides a complete causal mechanism — and every constant of physics is now derived directly from the requirement that observers exist
It refutes the existence of observers — and is widely understood to be a logical contradiction with no remaining defenders
It demonstrates that constants are random — and confirms there is no fine-tuning at all in any physical parameter
questions.context: The 'weak' anthropic principle (we observe a universe compatible with our existence — tautological but real) is uncontroversial. The 'strong' version (the universe was somehow constrained to produce observers) shades into theology or multiverse selection. Critics argue 'we exist, therefore constants permit existence' is descriptive, not explanatory. The relationship between the cosmological-constant problem, multiverse hypotheses, and the anthropic principle remains genuinely contested in current physics.

questions.question: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) — the formation of the lightest atomic nuclei in the first few minutes after the Big Bang — predicts very specific ratios of hydrogen, helium-4, deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7 in primordial gas. Astronomers measure these ratios in low-metallicity stars and primordial gas clouds. What is the overall result of comparing BBN predictions to observations?
questions.answer: BBN predictions match observations to high precision for hydrogen, helium-4, and deuterium — though the lithium-7 measurement has an unresolved discrepancy known as the 'lithium problem'
choices: BBN predictions match observations to high precision for hydrogen, helium-4, and deuterium — though the lithium-7 measurement has an unresolved discrepancy known as the 'lithium problem'
BBN predictions match nothing — every primordial-abundance measurement contradicts every prediction and Big Bang cosmology has been refuted
BBN predictions match perfectly for every nucleus — including lithium-7, with no remaining anomaly of any kind in any element
BBN predictions have never been compared to observation — and no primordial-abundance measurements have been published
questions.context: BBN is one of the standard model's great successes — three independent precision predictions (H, He-4, D abundances) all match observation within a few percent across many independent measurements. The lithium-7 measurement is consistently a factor of 2-3 below prediction — the 'cosmological lithium problem.' Possible explanations include uncertainty in stellar destruction of lithium, new particle physics, or sociological factors in primordial-gas measurements. Honest open puzzle within a broadly successful framework.

questions.question: Two independent methods for measuring the Hubble constant — the universe's current expansion rate — give different answers. The cosmic microwave background method (Planck satellite, 2018) gives about 67.4 km/s/Mpc. The local-distance-ladder method (using Type Ia supernovae and Cepheid variables, Adam Riess's SH0ES collaboration) gives about 73.0 km/s/Mpc. What does this 'Hubble tension' represent?
questions.answer: A persistent ~5 km/s/Mpc disagreement at >5-sigma significance — neither dismissable as random error nor explained by any established alternative model
choices: A persistent ~5 km/s/Mpc disagreement at >5-sigma significance — neither dismissable as random error nor explained by any established alternative model
A trivial measurement error of less than 0.01 km/s/Mpc — and there is no remaining tension between the methods at any meaningful precision
A historical curiosity from the 1990s — both methods now agree perfectly and the Hubble tension is no longer discussed in modern cosmology
A theoretical impossibility — and one of the two methods has been definitively retracted by its authors after independent reviewer challenges
questions.context: The Hubble tension is a major active puzzle in cosmology. Possible explanations include systematic errors in one or both methods (which careful work has not yet revealed), new physics in the early universe (early dark energy, different neutrino properties), or changes to the standard cosmological model. The Webb telescope's calibration of Cepheid distances tightened rather than relaxed the tension. Honest open question.

questions.question: Cosmology in the mid-2020s simultaneously has tremendous successes (the cosmic microwave background match, Big Bang nucleosynthesis precision, large-scale structure agreement) and significant open puzzles (dark matter identity, dark energy nature, the Hubble tension, JWST early galaxies, the cosmological-constant problem). How should a kid honestly characterize the state of the field?
questions.answer: The standard model works impressively across many tests but has named open puzzles that may require new physics — confident on many things, genuinely uncertain on others
choices: The standard model works impressively across many tests but has named open puzzles that may require new physics — confident on many things, genuinely uncertain on others
The standard model is fully complete — and there are no remaining open puzzles of any kind in cosmology as of the present day
The standard model has been completely overturned — and there is no working framework left in modern cosmology at any level
The standard model has never existed in cosmology — there is no agreement on any aspect of how the universe works
questions.context: LambdaCDM (the standard cosmological model with cold dark matter and a cosmological constant) is the working framework. It successfully predicts CMB anisotropies, large-scale structure statistics, BBN abundances. But it does not explain WHAT dark matter or dark energy IS, it does not resolve the Hubble tension, and it has not fully accommodated JWST observations. This is what mature science looks like — predictive success in a framework that openly names what it still doesn't know.

questions.question: Lake Vostok lies buried under about 4 kilometers of ice beneath the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. The lake has been sealed from the surface for an estimated 15-25 million years. Russian and other teams have drilled toward and into the lake since the 1990s. What is the central scientific concern about these drilling efforts?
questions.answer: Drilling fluids and surface organisms risk contaminating an isolated ecosystem before its native life can be characterized — a one-shot experiment that cannot be undone
choices: Drilling fluids and surface organisms risk contaminating an isolated ecosystem before its native life can be characterized — a one-shot experiment that cannot be undone
Drilling is impossible at any depth — and no team has ever managed to reach the lake despite repeated international efforts
Drilling has no contamination risk — Antarctic isolation makes any introduced organism impossible to survive at depth
Drilling has been universally celebrated — and no environmental concerns have ever been raised by any scientific body about the project
questions.context: The Russian team using kerosene-and-Freon drilling fluid reached the lake surface in February 2012. Subsequent analyses (Lukin, Bulat, Shtarkman, others) found bacterial DNA in samples, but distinguishing native organisms from drilling-fluid contaminants has been contested. The episode is a cautionary tale: a 25-million-year-isolated ecosystem deserved more contamination-control rigor than was applied. Honest science includes acknowledging methodological lapses.

questions.question: On September 1, 1859, English astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots through his observatory telescope when he witnessed an enormous solar flare — the largest geomagnetic storm in recorded history. What were the documented effects of the Carrington Event on Victorian infrastructure?
questions.answer: Telegraph systems failed across Europe and North America — some sparked fires, some operators received electric shocks, and aurorae appeared as far south as the Caribbean
choices: Telegraph systems failed across Europe and North America — some sparked fires, some operators received electric shocks, and aurorae appeared as far south as the Caribbean
Telegraph systems were unaffected — the event passed without any technological consequences because Victorian electronics were too primitive to interact with the storm
Telegraph systems received clearer signals — the storm boosted communications across continents and was celebrated by operators worldwide
Telegraph systems did not exist in 1859 — and Carrington witnessed only a small visual phenomenon with no infrastructure implications
questions.context: Telegraph operators in Boston and Portland reportedly disconnected their batteries and continued sending messages using the induced current from the storm itself. A modern Carrington-class event would impact a vastly larger electrical grid — power transformers, satellites, GPS, communication systems all vulnerable. The 2008 NASA STEREO mission observed a near-miss Carrington-class CME that passed Earth's orbit by about one week. Realistic risk worth naming.

questions.question: Earth's geological record contains evidence of many full reversals of the planet's magnetic field — periods where magnetic north and south swap. Paleomagnetic data preserved in volcanic rocks and ocean-floor magnetic stripes document hundreds of reversals over geological time. The most recent full reversal was the Brunhes-Matuyama transition about 780,000 years ago. How should reversals be characterized?
questions.answer: Geologically routine — multiple reversals per million years on average, with no documented mass-extinction correlation, though potential modern technological vulnerability
choices: Geologically routine — multiple reversals per million years on average, with no documented mass-extinction correlation, though potential modern technological vulnerability
Geologically extinct — no reversal has been documented in any record and the field has been stable since Earth formed
Geologically catastrophic — every reversal in the record corresponds to a complete mass extinction with universal species loss
Geologically uniform — the field has remained exactly the same throughout the entire 4.5 billion years of Earth's history
questions.context: Paleomagnetic data show roughly 4-5 full reversals per million years on average, though intervals vary widely. The current 'stable' interval (Brunhes chron, ~780,000 years and counting) is somewhat long by historical standards. Geomagnetic-pole drift has accelerated recently — the magnetic north pole has moved hundreds of kilometers across the Arctic since the 19th century. Whether we are approaching a reversal is genuinely open. No documented mass-extinction correlation in the record.

questions.question: Yellowstone's caldera is a known supervolcano. The most recent caldera-forming eruption was the Lava Creek eruption about 631,000 years ago, which produced the Yellowstone Caldera itself. Documentaries and popular media often frame Yellowstone as a near-term catastrophic threat. What is the actual best scientific framing of the realistic risk?
questions.answer: A caldera-scale eruption is possible over geological timescales but currently has a very low probability per year — many smaller eruptive events are far more likely
choices: A caldera-scale eruption is possible over geological timescales but currently has a very low probability per year — many smaller eruptive events are far more likely
A caldera-scale eruption is imminent within the current decade — and government documents have officially predicted catastrophe by a specific date
A caldera-scale eruption has been ruled out forever — and Yellowstone is geologically dormant with no remaining magma activity
A caldera-scale eruption is happening right now — and the ongoing event has been concealed from the public by federal agencies
questions.context: USGS monitoring of Yellowstone is extensive: seismic networks, GPS deformation, gas chemistry, hydrothermal surveys. The probability of a caldera-scale eruption in any given year is on the order of 1 in 730,000 by USGS estimates — far lower than many media presentations imply. Smaller hydrothermal explosions, modest lava flows, and steam events occur much more frequently. Genuine but extremely low-probability long-term concern, not an imminent threat.

questions.question: The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone — about 2,600 square kilometers around the failed reactor in northern Ukraine — was depopulated after the April 1986 disaster. Decades later, wildlife biologists including Tim Mousseau (University of South Carolina) and Sergey Gaschak (Chernobyl Center) have documented an outcome that is uncomfortable to articulate. What have the post-disaster wildlife surveys actually found?
questions.answer: Wildlife populations in the Exclusion Zone are higher than in comparable inhabited areas — radiation harm appears smaller than the harm caused by human presence itself
choices: Wildlife populations in the Exclusion Zone are higher than in comparable inhabited areas — radiation harm appears smaller than the harm caused by human presence itself
Wildlife populations in the Exclusion Zone are completely absent — no living animal has been documented within the zone since 1986
Wildlife populations in the Exclusion Zone match exactly nearby inhabited areas — radiation has no detectable effect on any species at all
Wildlife populations in the Exclusion Zone have not been studied — no researchers have entered the zone since the disaster
questions.context: The 30-plus years of wildlife observation in the Exclusion Zone is genuinely complicated. Some studies (Mousseau) document developmental abnormalities, reduced bird brain sizes, and lower insect populations. Other studies (Smith, Beresford, Gaschak) document thriving wolf, lynx, bear, elk, boar, and waterfowl populations. The honest summary: radiation effects are real but smaller, in net effect, than the chronic stressors of human presence — agriculture, hunting, road traffic, habitat destruction.
